messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Sexual assault
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Emotional Stress: Situations that make me feel strong emotions, Counterfactual Thinking: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred, Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Memory Gaps: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Vignette:
Amara is a 35-year-old Ethiopian American woman who has served as a police officer for nine years. She is married and lives with her husband in a mid-sized city where she grew up, surrounded by an extended family network and an Ethiopian Orthodox church community that had, until recently, been the organizing centre of her social world. She presented for therapy eight months after being sexually assaulted by a colleague during an after-shift gathering at a fellow officer's home.

The assault occurred in a back room of the house while others were socializing nearby. The man was someone Amara had worked alongside for three years, someone she had trusted. At one point during the assault she had tried to pull away and he had pressed his full weight against her, and the physical force of that — the specific pressure against her hips and lower back — became lodged in her body in a way she could not afterward explain or control. She remembered the ambient noise of the party continuing on the other side of the wall. She remembered the smell of alcohol. There were other details from those minutes that she could not retrieve no matter how carefully she tried to reconstruct them, and the blankness where memory should have been was itself a source of distress — a gap she could not account for and therefore could not close.

In the weeks that followed, the memories that did return came with a physical dimension that shocked her. When an intrusive image surfaced — and they came often, without warning — she felt the same concentrated pressure in her hips and lower back that she had felt during the assault itself. The physical sensation arrived alongside an intensity of rage that she described as almost dissociative in quality, a fury so large and sudden that it frightened her. She had not expected the rage. She had expected grief, or fear, or shame. The anger felt ungovernable, and she had come to believe that experiencing it at all was evidence of how fundamentally altered she now was.

That belief — that she had been permanently changed for the worse — had become one of the most fixed features of her inner life. She was certain that something essential had been damaged in her, that the woman who had walked into that gathering was gone and had been replaced by someone lesser, someone reactive and closed. She found herself returning again and again to a particular kind of thinking: that another woman, someone more alert or more cautious or simply luckier in her choices, would never have ended up in that room. She turned the evening over compulsively, revising it, imagining the version of her life in which she had left early, or had not gone at all, or had never trusted him. These revisions brought no relief, only a sharpened sense of what had been lost.

Her relationship to her community had quietly collapsed. She stopped attending church, first occasionally and then entirely. Her mother called; she answered less. She told herself she was tired, but what she was actually doing was steering away from any situation that might produce strong emotion — the warmth of a shared meal, the particular kind of love her church community expressed through physical closeness and collective prayer — because she could not predict what her body or her feelings might do in response. She also began avoiding any situation that carried the possibility of conflict or disagreement, including the ordinary friction of her marriage. Her husband noticed the distance and named it; she deflected. The deflections accumulated into a silence between them that had not existed before.

At work, the avoidance had taken on a specific and consequential shape. Amara was required to respond to calls involving sexual violence, and she had begun requesting reassignments without explanation, accepting the sideways looks from colleagues, saying nothing. Her supervisor had recently asked her directly whether she was managing, and the question — the confrontation implicit in it — had sent her to the bathroom, where she stood with her back against the wall for several minutes before returning to her desk.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a single event but an accumulation: the growing distance from her husband, the recognition that she was disappearing from her own life, and a quiet, persistent fear that she would never find her way back to the person she had been. What she hoped for, she said in the first session, was to stop feeling like a stranger inside her own marriage, her own community, her own skin. What she feared most was that it was already too late for that.
